chapter_note.about: Trigonometry measures angles and the circle. This chapter rebuilds five ideas from zero: radians, sine and cosine as the coordinates of a point on the unit circle, tangent and the standard values, the key identities, and the graphs. Calculus treats $\sin$ and $\cos$ as functions of an angle in radians, so limits, Taylor series and integrals all assume this chapter. It also lies behind the rotation matrices in linear algebra. Each card starts from a picture of the unit circle and ends with a GATE-shaped question.
chapter_note.simple: Picture a bicycle wheel of radius 1 with a valve on the rim. Turn the wheel by an angle: the valve's height is the sine, and its distance sideways from the centre is the cosine. Tangent is the slope of the line from the hub to the valve. Because the valve stays on the rim, height squared plus sideways squared is always 1. Plot the height as the wheel turns and you get a smooth wave that repeats every full turn. Calculus measures these angles in radians, where a half turn is $\pi$.

cards.title: Radians
cards.simple: A degree cuts a full turn into 360 slices. A radian is a different way to measure the same turn: walk along the edge of a circle until your path is exactly as long as the radius. The angle at the centre for that walk is 1 radian, about 57 degrees. A full turn is that walk repeated about 6.28 times, which is $2\pi$. So half a turn is $\pi$ radians and a quarter turn is $\frac\pi2$. Calculus needs radians because they connect an angle straight to distance along the circle. In exam words: $180^\circ=\pi$ radians, and on a circle of radius $r$ the arc length is $s=r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians.
cards.idea: A **radian** measures an angle by the length of the arc it cuts on a circle of radius 1. A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so $180^\circ=\pi$ rad. On a circle of radius $r$, an angle of $\theta$ radians cuts an arc of length $r\theta$. Calculus and the series for $\sin$ and $\cos$ only work in radians.
cards.definition:
$$\text{radians}=\text{degrees}\times\frac\pi{180},\qquad s=r\theta$$

Benchmarks: $30^\circ=\frac\pi6$, $45^\circ=\frac\pi4$, $60^\circ=\frac\pi3$, $90^\circ=\frac\pi2$, $180^\circ=\pi$, $360^\circ=2\pi$. One radian is about $57.3^\circ$. Symbols: $\theta$ is the angle in radians, $r$ the radius and $s$ the arc length.
cards.intuition_full: A radian is a ratio: arc length divided by radius. That makes it a pure number with no units, which is why it fits so smoothly into formulas. For a small angle, the arc and the height of the point above the x-axis are almost equal, so $\sin\theta\approx\theta$. This is true only when $\theta$ is in radians. It is the reason $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}x=1$ in the calculus chapters. To convert, remember $\pi=180^\circ$ and use ratios: $45^\circ$ is a quarter of $180^\circ$, so it is $\frac\pi4$. Angles bigger than $2\pi$ simply wrap around, and negative angles turn clockwise.

examples.setup: Convert $60^\circ$ to radians and find the arc it cuts on the unit circle.
steps: A full turn is $360^\circ$, and the unit circle's edge is $2\pi$ long. So $360^\circ=2\pi$ radians.
On the unit circle the arc cut by this angle has length $\frac\pi3\approx1.047$: arc length equals the angle in radians.
One radian (arc equal to the radius) is about $57.3^\circ$, a little less than $60^\circ$.

examples.setup: A wheel of radius 20 cm turns through $135^\circ$. How far does a point on the rim travel?
examples.answer: About $47.1$ cm. The trap avoided: using $s=20\cdot135$ with degrees.

examples.setup: Compare $\sin(0.1)$ with $\sin(0.1^\circ)$. When is the shortcut $\sin x\approx x$ valid?
steps: So $\sin x\approx x$ holds only when $x$ is in **radians**.

cards.what_full:
A **radian** measures an angle by the length of the arc it cuts on a circle of radius 1. A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so $180^\circ=\pi$ rad. On a circle of radius $r$, an angle of $\theta$ radians cuts an arc of length $r\theta$. Calculus and the series for $\sin$ and $\cos$ only work in radians.

$$\text{radians}=\text{degrees}\times\frac\pi{180},\qquad s=r\theta$$

Benchmarks: $30^\circ=\frac\pi6$, $45^\circ=\frac\pi4$, $60^\circ=\frac\pi3$, $90^\circ=\frac\pi2$, $180^\circ=\pi$, $360^\circ=2\pi$. One radian is about $57.3^\circ$. Symbols: $\theta$ is the angle in radians, $r$ the radius and $s$ the arc length.

**Worked example.** Convert $60^\circ$ to radians and find the arc it cuts on the unit circle.

1. A full turn is $360^\circ$, and the unit circle's edge is $2\pi$ long. So $360^\circ=2\pi$ radians.
2. $60^\circ$ is $\frac{60}{360}=\frac16$ of a full turn.
3. $60^\circ=\frac16\cdot2\pi=\frac\pi3\approx1.047$ radians.
4. On the unit circle the arc cut by this angle has length $\frac\pi3\approx1.047$: arc length equals the angle in radians.
5. One radian (arc equal to the radius) is about $57.3^\circ$, a little less than $60^\circ$.

**Answer:** $60^\circ=\frac\pi3\approx1.047$ radians.

cards.title: Sine and cosine on the unit circle
cards.simple: Imagine a bicycle wheel of radius 1 with a valve on the rim. Spin it and look at the valve from two sides. From the side you see how high it is, and from above you see how far it is from the hub sideways. Sine is the height and cosine is the sideways distance. At $0^\circ$ the valve is at the front ($\cos=1$, $\sin=0$), and at $90^\circ$ it is at the top ($\cos=0$, $\sin=1$). Past $90^\circ$ the valve is behind the hub, so cosine goes negative, and below the hub sine goes negative. In exam words: the point at angle $\theta$ on the unit circle is $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$.
cards.idea: Draw a circle of radius 1 centred at the origin. Turn through an angle $\theta$ from the positive x-axis and you land on the point **$(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$**. Cosine is the horizontal position and sine is the vertical position. This works for every angle, past $90^\circ$ too, and it hands you the signs for free.
cards.definition:
$$P(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta),\qquad -1\le\sin\theta\le1,\quad -1\le\cos\theta\le1$$

Signs by quadrant: Quadrant I: $\sin+$, $\cos+$. Quadrant II ($90^\circ$ to $180^\circ$): $\sin+$, $\cos-$. Quadrant III: both $-$. Quadrant IV: $\cos+$, $\sin-$. Axis points: $(1,0)$ at $0^\circ$, $(0,1)$ at $90^\circ$, $(-1,0)$ at $180^\circ$, $(0,-1)$ at $270^\circ$.
cards.intuition_full: In a right triangle, $\sin=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$. On the unit circle the hypotenuse is 1, so the sine is just the opposite side, the height. The circle extends the idea beyond $90^\circ$, where triangles stop making sense. Mirror symmetry gives shortcuts: $150^\circ$ is the mirror of $30^\circ$ in the y-axis, so it has the same height but the opposite sideways position. The **reference angle** is the acute angle between the radius and the x-axis. The size of $\sin$ and $\cos$ comes from the reference angle, and the signs come from the quadrant. After a full turn the point returns to the start, so both functions repeat every $2\pi$ ($360^\circ$).

examples.setup: Track the point at $30^\circ,\ 90^\circ,\ 150^\circ,\ 210^\circ,\ 330^\circ$ and record $(\cos,\sin)$.
steps: $90^\circ$: $(0,\ 1)$. The point is at the top.
examples.answer: $\sin$ is positive in quadrants I and II; $\cos$ is positive in quadrants I and IV.

examples.setup: How many angles $\theta$ in $[0,2\pi]$ satisfy $\sin\theta=\frac12$? Find them.
steps: $\sin\theta$ is the height. Draw the line $y=\frac12$. It cuts the circle at two points.
One is in quadrant I: reference angle $\frac\pi6$, so $\theta=\frac\pi6$.
The other is its mirror in the y-axis: $\theta=\pi-\frac\pi6=\frac{5\pi}6$.
examples.answer: Two solutions, $\frac\pi6$ and $\frac{5\pi}6$. The trap avoided: giving only $30^\circ$.

Draw a circle of radius 1 centred at the origin. Turn through an angle $\theta$ from the positive x-axis and you land on the point **$(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$**. $$P(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta),\qquad -1\le\sin\theta\le1,\quad -1\le\cos\theta\le1$$

**Worked example.** Track the point at $30^\circ,\ 90^\circ,\ 150^\circ,\ 210^\circ,\ 330^\circ$ and record $(\cos,\sin)$.

1. $30^\circ$: $(\cos,\sin)=(0.866,\ 0.5)$. Both positive.
2. $90^\circ$: $(0,\ 1)$. The point is at the top.
3. $150^\circ$: $(-0.866,\ 0.5)$. Same height as $30^\circ$, mirrored sideways.
4. $210^\circ$: $(-0.866,\ -0.5)$. Both negative.
5. $330^\circ$: $(0.866,\ -0.5)$. $\cos$ positive, $\sin$ negative.

**Answer:** $\sin$ is positive in quadrants I and II; $\cos$ is positive in quadrants I and IV.

cards.title: Tangent and the standard values
cards.simple: Tangent is the slope of the line from the hub to the valve: how much it rises for each step across. If sine is the height and cosine is the sideways distance, then the slope is height divided by sideways, so $\tan=\sin\div\cos$. At $45^\circ$ the valve is as high as it is far across, so the slope is 1. At $30^\circ$ it is flatter, slope about 0.58. At $60^\circ$ it is steeper, about 1.73. At $90^\circ$ the line goes straight up and the slope does not exist. In exam words: $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, and you should know the exact values at $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.
cards.idea: **Tangent** is sine divided by cosine: the slope of the radius. A handful of angles come up again and again: $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$. Their sines, cosines and tangents are easy to recall from a pattern.
cards.intuition_full: Memory trick: write the sines at $0,30,45,60,90$ as $\frac{\sqrt0}2,\frac{\sqrt1}2,\frac{\sqrt2}2,\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac{\sqrt4}2$. The cosines are the same list backwards. Then tangent is one divided by the other. The word tangent comes from the picture: the line $x=1$ touches the circle at $(1,0)$, and extending the radius until it hits that line gives the height $\tan\theta$. As the angle nears $90^\circ$, the radius becomes vertical and never meets the line, so the height blows up. Since $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and both signs flip together after a half turn, $\tan$ repeats every $\pi$, not $2\pi$. For angles outside the first quadrant, use the reference angle and fix the sign.

examples.setup: Find $\tan45^\circ$ and complete the table of $\sin,\cos,\tan$ at $30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ$.
steps: Pattern: $\sin$ is $\frac{\sqrt1}2,\frac{\sqrt2}2,\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $\cos$ is that list reversed.
examples.answer: $\tan45^\circ=1$; the full table is as above.

steps: $150^\circ$ is in quadrant II with reference angle $30^\circ$: $\sin150^\circ=+\frac12$.
$300^\circ$ is in quadrant IV with reference angle $60^\circ$: $\cos300^\circ=+\frac12$.
$225^\circ$ is in quadrant III with reference angle $45^\circ$: $\tan225^\circ=+1$ (both $\sin$ and $\cos$ negative, so the ratio is positive).
examples.answer: $\frac54=1.25$. The trap avoided: giving $\tan225^\circ$ a minus sign.

examples.setup: Why is $\tan90^\circ$ undefined? What happens to $\tan\theta$ just below $90^\circ$?
steps: As $\theta\to90^\circ$ from below, $\tan\theta$ grows without limit.
examples.answer: $\tan90^\circ$ is undefined; just below $90^\circ$ the tangent is huge and positive.

cards.why: These exact values appear whenever a question uses $\frac\pi6$, $\frac\pi4$ or $\frac\pi3$. Tangent is also the slope of a line at a given angle, which links trig to straight lines and later to derivatives. In GATE: exact trig values, slopes from angles, and angle reduction.
how: For an unusual angle, find its reference angle (30, 45 or 60 degrees).
Recall $\sin$ and $\cos$ of the reference angle from the $\frac{\sqrt n}2$ pattern.
Fix the sign by quadrant.
For $\tan$, divide $\sin$ by $\cos$.
cards.mistake: Swapping the $\sin$ and $\cos$ columns between $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, or saying $\tan30^\circ=\frac12$ (that is $\sin30^\circ$). Also forgetting that $\tan$ is undefined at $90^\circ$.
edge_cases: $\tan\theta$ blows up at odd multiples of $90^\circ$.
connections: found.derivatives: the slope of a curve is a tangent of an angle.

cards.what_full:
**Tangent** is sine divided by cosine: the slope of the radius. A handful of angles come up again and again: $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$. Their sines, cosines and tangents are easy to recall from a pattern.

$$\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$$

| $\theta$ | $0$ | $30^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin$ | $0$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}2$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ | $1$ |
| $\cos$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}2$ | $\frac12$ | $0$ |
| $\tan$ | $0$ | $\frac1{\sqrt3}$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | undefined |

$\tan$ is undefined wherever $\cos\theta=0$.

**Worked example.** Find $\tan45^\circ$ and complete the table of $\sin,\cos,\tan$ at $30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ$.

1. At $45^\circ$: $\sin=\cos=\frac{\sqrt2}2\approx0.707$.
2. $\tan45^\circ=\frac{\sin}{\cos}=1$. The radius meets $x=1$ at height 1.
3. At $30^\circ$: $\sin=\frac12$, $\cos=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $\tan=\frac1{\sqrt3}$.
4. At $60^\circ$: $\sin=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $\cos=\frac12$, $\tan=\sqrt3$.
5. Pattern: $\sin$ is $\frac{\sqrt1}2,\frac{\sqrt2}2,\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $\cos$ is that list reversed.

**Answer:** $\tan45^\circ=1$; the full table is as above.

Foundation — used in: calc.limits, found.derivatives, la.eigen, ml.logreg, ml.svm.

cards.title: Key identities
cards.simple: The valve of the wheel always sits on the rim, 1 unit from the hub. That single fact gives the most important identity in trig. The sideways distance and the height are the two short sides of a right triangle, and the radius, 1, is the longest side. Pythagoras says short squared plus short squared equals long squared. So $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$, always. If you know one of them you can find the other: if the height is 0.6, then the sideways distance squared is $1-0.36=0.64$, so it is 0.8 (the 3-4-5 triangle in disguise). Other identities describe symmetries of the circle. In exam words: $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$.
cards.idea: Because $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ sits on a circle of radius 1, $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ for every angle. From this fact, plus the symmetry of the circle, come the identities you need: negative angles, supplementary angles and double angles. Identities let you swap a hard expression for an easy one.
cards.definition:
$$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,\qquad \tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$$

Symmetry: $\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta$, $\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta$, $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$, $\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta$, $\sin(\tfrac\pi2-\theta)=\cos\theta$.

Double angle: $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, and $\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$.

Sum: $\sin(a+b)=\sin a\cos b+\cos a\sin b$, $\cos(a+b)=\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin b$.
cards.intuition_full: The symmetry rules are mirror pictures. Replacing $\theta$ by $-\theta$ reflects the point in the x-axis, so the height flips sign and the sideways position stays. Replacing $\theta$ by $\pi-\theta$ reflects it in the y-axis, so the height stays and the sideways position flips. The double-angle formula $\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta$ rearranges to $1-\cos2\theta=2\sin^2\theta$, which is the key to many limits and integrals. When you need $\cos\theta$ from $\sin\theta$, the identity gives $\cos\theta=\pm\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}$. The sign is decided by the quadrant. A test angle like $30^\circ$ or $0$ quickly exposes a wrongly remembered formula.

examples.setup: $\sin\theta=\frac35$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant. Find $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$.
steps: Draw the line at height $0.6$. It meets the circle at the point for $\theta$.
The legs $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ and the radius 1 form a right triangle.
Use $\cos x=1-2\sin^2\frac x2$, so $1-\cos x=2\sin^2\frac x2$.
As $x\to0$, $\frac x2\to0$ and $\frac{\sin u}u\to1$ (with $u=\frac x2$ in radians).
examples.answer: $\frac12$. The trap avoided: expecting $\frac00$ to mean 0 or no limit.

examples.setup: $\sin\theta=\frac35$ again, but now $\theta$ is in the second quadrant. Find $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$.
steps: In the second quadrant the point is left of the y-axis, so $\cos\theta<0$.
examples.answer: $\cos\theta=-\frac45$ and $\tan\theta=-\frac34$. The same $\sin$ leads to two angles, $\theta$ and $\pi-\theta$.

cards.why: Identities turn an awkward expression into an easy one, so that a limit, integral or equation becomes quick. In GATE: simplify $\sin^2+\cos^2$, use $1-\cos x=2\sin^2\frac x2$ in limits, use $\sin2\theta$ in rotation matrices, and use $\cos2x$ to integrate $\sin^2x$.
how: Look for $\sin^2+\cos^2$ and replace it by 1.
Use $\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$ to remove squares.
To find $\cos$ from $\sin$, use $\cos=\pm\sqrt{1-\sin^2}$ and pick the sign by quadrant.
Test with an easy angle such as $30^\circ$ or $0$.
cards.mistake: Forgetting the $\pm$ and the quadrant sign, and writing $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta$. At $\theta=30^\circ$: $\sin60^\circ=0.866$ but $2\sin30^\circ=1$. The double-angle formula has a $\cos\theta$ factor too.
edge_cases: Identities hold for every $\theta$. One angle is enough to catch a mistake.
connections: la.eigen: $R(\theta)^2=R(2\theta)$ for rotation matrices uses the double-angle formulas.

From this fact, plus the symmetry of the circle, come the identities you need: negative angles, supplementary angles and double angles. Identities let you swap a hard expression for an easy one.

$$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,\qquad \tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$$

Symmetry: $\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta$, $\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta$, $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$, $\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta$, $\sin(\tfrac\pi2-\theta)=\cos\theta$.

Double angle: $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, and $\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$.

Sum: $\sin(a+b)=\sin a\cos b+\cos a\sin b$, $\cos(a+b)=\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin b$.

**Worked example.** $\sin\theta=\frac35$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant. Find $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$.

1. Draw the line at height $0.6$. It meets the circle at the point for $\theta$.
2. The legs $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ and the radius 1 form a right triangle.
3. Pythagoras: $0.6^2+\cos^2\theta=1$, so $\cos^2\theta=1-0.36=0.64$.
4. First quadrant means $\cos\theta>0$, so $\cos\theta=0.8$.
5. $\tan\theta=\frac{0.6}{0.8}=0.75$.

**Answer:** $\cos\theta=\frac45$ and $\tan\theta=\frac34$.
cards.why_full:
Identities turn an awkward expression into an easy one, so that a limit, integral or equation becomes quick. In GATE: simplify $\sin^2+\cos^2$, use $1-\cos x=2\sin^2\frac x2$ in limits, use $\sin2\theta$ in rotation matrices, and use $\cos2x$ to integrate $\sin^2x$.

Foundation — used in: calc.limits, calc.taylor, calc.mvt_integration, la.eigen, la.proj.
cards.trap: Forgetting the $\pm$ and the quadrant sign, and writing $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta$. At $\theta=30^\circ$: $\sin60^\circ=0.866$ but $2\sin30^\circ=1$. The double-angle formula has a $\cos\theta$ factor too.

cards.title: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
cards.simple: Ride the valve around the wheel while a pen records its height as the wheel turns. The pen draws a smooth wave. It starts in the middle, climbs to 1, comes back to the middle, dips to $-1$, and returns. Then it repeats forever. One full repeat takes one full turn, $2\pi$. Cosine is the same wave started a quarter-turn earlier, so it is the sine wave shifted left by $\frac\pi2$. Tangent is the slope of the radius, so it explodes at $90^\circ$ and repeats every half turn. In exam words: $y=\sin\theta$ and $y=\cos\theta$ have period $2\pi$ and range $[-1,1]$, while $\tan\theta$ has period $\pi$.
cards.idea: The graph of **$\sin\theta$** records the height of a point going round the unit circle: a smooth wave with period $2\pi$ and range $[-1,1]$. **$\cos\theta$** is the same wave shifted left by $\frac\pi2$. **$\tan\theta$** has period $\pi$ and vertical asymptotes wherever $\cos\theta=0$.
cards.definition:
$$\sin(\theta+2\pi)=\sin\theta,\qquad \cos\theta=\sin\!\left(\theta+\tfrac\pi2\right),\qquad \tan(\theta+\pi)=\tan\theta$$

For $y=A\sin(B\theta)$: **amplitude** $|A|$ (the height of the wave) and **period** $\frac{2\pi}{|B|}$. Key points of $\sin$: $0$ at $0,\pi,2\pi$; maximum 1 at $\frac\pi2$; minimum $-1$ at $\frac{3\pi}2$. Zeros of $\sin$ are at $n\pi$; zeros of $\cos$ are at $\frac\pi2+n\pi$.
cards.intuition_full: The graph is the unit circle unrolled: the x-axis of the graph measures the angle (arc length) and the height measures $\sin$. Sine is odd (symmetric through the origin) and cosine is even (mirror-symmetric about the y-axis), just like $x^3$ and $x^2$ in the functions chapter. The shifting and stretching rules apply directly: $3\sin(2\theta)$ is the basic wave stretched up by 3 and squeezed sideways by 2, so its period halves to $\pi$. Over one full period the positive and negative parts of $\sin$ cancel, so its average is 0. That is the reason $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin x\,dx=0$. Tangent is $\frac{\sin}{\cos}$, so it has an asymptote wherever $\cos=0$.

examples.setup: Plot $y=\sin\theta$ at $\theta=0,\frac\pi2,\pi,\frac{3\pi}2,2\pi$ and then compare with $\cos\theta$.
steps: $\theta=2\pi$: height 0, back at the start. The wave repeats, period $2\pi$.
$\cos\theta=\sin(\theta+\frac\pi2)$ is the same wave shifted left by $\frac\pi2$.

examples.setup: Find the period and the range of $f(x)=3\sin(2x)$.
steps: The factor 3 outside stretches the heights: amplitude 3, so the range is $[-3,3]$.
The 2 inside squeezes the wave sideways by 2: period $=\frac{2\pi}2=\pi$.
Check: $f(0)=0$, $f(\frac\pi4)=3\sin\frac\pi2=3$ (the maximum), $f(\frac\pi2)=3\sin\pi=0$, $f(\pi)=3\sin2\pi=0$, and the pattern repeats after $\pi$.
examples.answer: Period $\pi$ and range $[-3,3]$. The trap avoided: saying the period is $4\pi$ or $2\pi\cdot2$.

examples.setup: What is the period of $\tan x$? Where is it undefined? Compare $\tan\frac\pi4$, $\tan\frac{3\pi}4$ and $\tan\frac{5\pi}4$.
steps: $\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ is undefined where $\cos x=0$: $x=\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}2,\dots$
$\tan\frac{5\pi}4=\frac{-\sqrt2/2}{-\sqrt2/2}=1$, the same as $\tan\frac\pi4$, a half-turn ($\pi$) later.
examples.answer: The period of $\tan$ is $\pi$, with asymptotes at odd multiples of $\frac\pi2$.

cards.why: The shapes of the trig graphs tell you where a function is zero, largest, increasing, and how often it repeats. In GATE: periods and ranges, zeros of $\sin$ and $\cos$, integrals of $\sin$ and $\cos$ over full periods (which are zero), and the sign of $\sin$ and $\cos$ on an interval.
how: Read off the amplitude $A$ and the period $\frac{2\pi}{B}$.
Mark the five key points of each period: start, quarter, half, three-quarters, end.
Apply shifts: inside the bracket moves sideways, with the opposite sign.
Use the picture for signs and zeros.
cards.mistake: Using degrees on the x-axis when the problem is in radians, or saying that $\sin2x$ has period $4\pi$. Doubling the speed halves the period to $\pi$. Another slip is forgetting that $\tan$ has period $\pi$.
edge_cases: $\sin$ and $\cos$ have range $[-1,1]$. $\tan$ has range all real numbers.
Zeros of $\sin$ are at $n\pi$. Zeros of $\cos$ are at $\frac\pi2+n\pi$.
The average of $\sin$ over a full period is 0.
connections: calc.mvt_integration: $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin x\,dx=0$. calc.taylor: $\sin x\approx x-\frac{x^3}6$ near 0.
found.functions: shifting and stretching rules apply to trig graphs.

cards.what_full:
The graph of **$\sin\theta$** records the height of a point going round the unit circle: a smooth wave with period $2\pi$ and range $[-1,1]$. **$\cos\theta$** is the same wave shifted left by $\frac\pi2$. **$\tan\theta$** has period $\pi$ and vertical asymptotes wherever $\cos\theta=0$.

$$\sin(\theta+2\pi)=\sin\theta,\qquad \cos\theta=\sin\!\left(\theta+\tfrac\pi2\right),\qquad \tan(\theta+\pi)=\tan\theta$$

For $y=A\sin(B\theta)$: **amplitude** $|A|$ (the height of the wave) and **period** $\frac{2\pi}{|B|}$. Key points of $\sin$: $0$ at $0,\pi,2\pi$; maximum 1 at $\frac\pi2$; minimum $-1$ at $\frac{3\pi}2$. Zeros of $\sin$ are at $n\pi$; zeros of $\cos$ are at $\frac\pi2+n\pi$.

**Worked example.** Plot $y=\sin\theta$ at $\theta=0,\frac\pi2,\pi,\frac{3\pi}2,2\pi$ and then compare with $\cos\theta$.

1. $\theta=0$: the point $(1,0)$ has height 0. Plot $(0,0)$.
2. $\theta=\frac\pi2$: height 1. Plot $(1.57,1)$.
3. $\theta=\pi$: height 0. Plot $(3.14,0)$.
4. $\theta=\frac{3\pi}2$: height $-1$. Plot $(4.71,-1)$.
5. $\theta=2\pi$: height 0, back at the start. The wave repeats, period $2\pi$.
6. $\cos\theta=\sin(\theta+\frac\pi2)$ is the same wave shifted left by $\frac\pi2$.

**Answer:** Heights $0,1,0,-1,0$ across one period of $2\pi$.

scenes.title: 60° as an arc of the unit circle

steps.caption: A full turn is $360^\circ$. The circle of radius 1 has an edge $2\pi$ long, so a full turn is $2\pi$ radians.
$60^\circ$ is $\frac{60}{360}=\frac16$ of a full turn.
So $60^\circ=\frac16\cdot2\pi=\frac\pi3\approx1.047$ radians.
On the unit circle the arc cut by this angle has length $\frac\pi3\approx1.047$. Arc length equals the angle in radians.
For comparison, 1 radian is an arc exactly as long as the radius. It is about $57.3^\circ$, a little less than $60^\circ$.

scenes.title: The point (cos θ, sin θ) travelling round the unit circle

steps.caption: At $30^\circ$ the point is $(\cos30^\circ,\sin30^\circ)=(0.866,\ 0.5)$. Its shadow on the x-axis is $\cos$, its height is $\sin$.
At $90^\circ$ the point is at the top: $\cos90^\circ=0$ and $\sin90^\circ=1$.
At $150^\circ$ the point is left of the y-axis: $\cos150^\circ=-0.866$, but the height is still $\sin150^\circ=0.5$.
At $210^\circ$ the point is below and to the left: both $\cos$ and $\sin$ are negative.
At $330^\circ$ the point is below but right of the y-axis: $\cos$ is positive and $\sin$ is negative.

scenes.title: tan θ as the height where the radius meets the tangent line x = 1

steps.caption: At $45^\circ$ the point is $(0.707,0.707)$, so $\sin45^\circ=\cos45^\circ=\frac{\sqrt2}2$.
$\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$. Here it is $\frac{0.707}{0.707}=1$. Extend the radius until it meets the tangent line $x=1$: it hits at height 1.
At $30^\circ$: $\sin=\frac12$, $\cos=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $\tan=\frac1{\sqrt3}\approx0.577$. The ray hits lower.
At $60^\circ$: $\sin=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $\cos=\frac12$, so $\tan=\sqrt3\approx1.732$. The ray hits higher.
The table is complete. Pattern: $\sin$ goes $\frac{\sqrt1}2,\frac{\sqrt2}2,\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $\cos$ is the same list reversed.

scenes.title: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 as a right triangle in the unit circle

steps.caption: We know $\sin\theta=\frac35=0.6$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant. Draw the line at height 0.6; it meets the circle at the point of angle $\theta$.
The point $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and the two legs form a right triangle. The hypotenuse is the radius, 1.

set.text:
right triangle
legs cos θ, sin θ
hypotenuse 1

steps.caption: Pythagoras: $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$, so $0.36+\cos^2\theta=1$ and $\cos^2\theta=0.64$.
In the first quadrant $\cos\theta>0$, so $\cos\theta=0.8$.
$\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{0.6}{0.8}=0.75$.

scenes.title: Unrolling the unit circle into y = sin θ

steps.caption: $\sin\theta$ is the height of the point on the circle. Start at $\theta=0$: the point is $(1,0)$, height 0. Record $(\theta,\sin\theta)=(0,0)$ on the graph.
$\theta=\frac\pi2\approx1.57$: the point is at the top, height 1. Plot $(1.57,\ 1)$.
$\theta=\pi\approx3.14$: the point is at $(-1,0)$, height 0. Plot $(3.14,\ 0)$.
$\theta=\frac{3\pi}2\approx4.71$: the point is at the bottom, height $-1$. Plot $(4.71,\ -1)$.
$\theta=2\pi\approx6.28$: back where we started, height 0. The wave now repeats: its period is $2\pi$.
$\cos\theta$ is the same wave shifted left by $\frac\pi2$: $\cos\theta=\sin(\theta+\frac\pi2)$. It starts at 1 instead of 0.

set.text:
cos θ = sin(θ + π/2)
